papers.title: Quantum error correction at ultra-low overhead
papers.abstract: Suppressing errors is the central challenge for useful large-scale quantum computing. While quantum error correction promises a viable solution to this challenge, existing codes typically suffer from trade-offs among encoding efficiency, error threshold, and hardware feasibility. Here, we introduce Cornucopia codes, a family of practical, hardware-efficient quantum low-density parity-check codes that achieve an ultra-high encoding rate exceeding $1/2$ while maintaining a pseudo-threshold exceeding $0.4\%$ under the standard circuit-level noise model. Inspired by recent affine-permutation-based code constructions and the long-range connectivity available in reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays, we adopt a structured code geometry in which the code layout, atom rearrangement, and syndrome-extraction schedule are co-designed. This structure enables nonlocal syndrome measurements through simple, parallel atom rearrangements. A complete syndrome extraction cycle measures all $X$- and $Z$-type checks in parallel with $12$ entangling layers, independent of the code size. The resulting threshold is comparable to those of the surface code and bivariate bicycle codes. In particular, a single code block $[[2844,1426,18]]$ encodes $1{,}426$ distance-$18$ logical qubits, achieving an extrapolated logical error rate of $2.6\times10^{-16}$ ($1.9\times10^{-31}$) per logical qubit per cycle, assuming the physical error rate of $0.1\%$ ($0.01\%$). By comparison, a bivariate bicycle code implementation would require more than $68{,}000$ physical qubits to encode the same number of logical qubits at a comparable logical error rate. These results bring demonstrations of ultra-low-overhead quantum error correction within the reach of near-term quantum processors.

summary.summary: Cornucopia codes are a family of quantum low-density parity-check codes achieving encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ while maintaining pseudo-thresholds above $0.4\%$ under circuit-level noise, designed for efficient implementation on reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays through co-optimized code geometry and atom-rearrangement protocols. A single $[[2844, 1426, 18]]$ code block encodes 1426 logical qubits with extrapolated logical error rates of $2.6 \times 10^{-16}$ per logical qubit per cycle at physical error rate $0.1\%$, achieving greater than tenfold reduction in qubit overhead compared to bivariate bicycle codes.
summary.motivation: Existing quantum error correction codes face fundamental trade-offs between encoding efficiency, error threshold, and hardware feasibility; reducing physical-qubit overhead without sacrificing fault tolerance is critical for scaling quantum computers.
summary.method: Cornucopia codes employ a block-convolutional construction with affine-permutation-based structure on a quasi-cyclic geometry $\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_q$, organizing 12 data blocks (six $L$-type and six $R$-type) and six check blocks, with syndrome extraction via 12 layers of transversal CNOTs that compile into simple parallel atom rearrangements (collective cyclic shifts and row permutations) compatible with acousto-optic deflectors.
summary.result: At $p = 10^{-3}$ physical error rate, the $[[2844, 1426, 18]]$ code achieves logical error rate $2.6 \times 10^{-16}$ per logical qubit per cycle using 4266 physical qubits, compared to 68,000+ qubits required by bivariate bicycle codes for equivalent performance; qubit-routing time per syndrome cycle is merely 16.18 ms, three orders of magnitude shorter than demonstrated neutral-atom coherence times of $\sim 10$ s.

papers.title: Time-optimal quantum gates with bang-bang control in multilevel systems
papers.abstract: We determine the optimal quantum manipulation protocols for implementing high-fidelity, fast single-qubit gates. We demonstrate that the time-optimal pulse sequence is a ``bang-bang'' sequence: discrete pulses of either positive or negative maximum amplitude or zero. The non-adiabatic bang-bang pulse sequence minimizes gate duration providing a speedup for low-frequency architectures. We first derive the protocol for a transversally driven two-level system, extracting exact analytic expressions for minimum gate times. We then extend this framework to general multilevel architectures, identifying conditions that enable the coherent suppression of leakage errors. Using the fluxonium circuit as a representative case study, we optimize $X/2$ and $Y/2$ gates through a combination of discrete bang sequences and continuous waveform smoothing. This approach preserves near-optimal execution speeds while mitigating transitions outside the computational subspace. Open-system simulations demonstrate that these sequences outperform commensurate and resonant pulse schemes across different fluxonium regimes, achieving low-error manipulation significantly faster than standard resonant control, even in the presence of $1/f$ flux noise and dissipation.

summary.summary: This work applies Pontryagin's Principle to determine time-optimal bang-bang pulse sequences for single-qubit $\pi/2$ gates, proving that the fastest implementation consists of discrete maximum-amplitude pulses alternating with idle periods. The framework is demonstrated on a transversally driven two-level system with exact analytic solutions, then extended to the fluxonium superconducting circuit where coherent suppression of leakage through interference conditions enables high-fidelity operation despite strong driving.
summary.motivation: Low-frequency superconducting qubits offer long coherence times but suffer from impractically slow gate durations under resonant control. Standard approaches break the rotating-wave approximation at strong drives, necessitating fundamental limits on achievable gate speeds in the non-adiabatic regime.
summary.method: Optimal control theory via Pontryagin's Principle constrains the control field $\phi(t)$ to bang-bang sequences: $\phi(t) \in \{\pm\phi_{\max}, 0\}$. For a TLS, analytic expressions are derived for minimum gate times as functions of $\phi/\Delta$. For fluxonium with parameters $E_C, E_L, E_J$, the optimization exploits selection rules in the phase operator to identify parameter regions where transitions to leakage states ($|0\rangle \leftrightarrow |3\rangle$, $|1\rangle \leftrightarrow |2\rangle$) destructively interfere, returning population to the computational subspace.
summary.result: For the Heavy fluxonium regime ($\Delta/2\pi = 14$ MHz, $\alpha = 214$), bang-bang $Y/2$ gates achieve $1-F \approx 10^{-4}$ in $t_g \approx 19$ ns approaching the theoretical bound $\tau_L/4 \approx 17.5$ ns, with average Clifford time $\bar{t}_g = 50.7$ ns outperforming resonant control at 108 ns; the asymmetric $X/2$ protocol delivers $1-F = 10^{-5}$ in 1.9 ns, reducing average time to 33 ns. Open-system simulations including $1/f$ flux noise with $\sigma = 5.21 \times 10^{-6}\Phi_0$ and dielectric loss ($T_1, T_2 \sim 200$–$300$ µs) confirm robustness across Heavy, Mid, and Light regimes.
